extracted.intended_audience: mathematical olympiad students and advanced problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Solving and writing rigorous solutions for olympiad-style number theory and combinatorics problems (proofs, constructions, modular arguments, digit/base reasoning). Emphasis on classical methods: congruences, induction, transformations, base expansions, and combinatorial counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude claims by induction on an integer parameter (e.g., 'Thus the claim follows by induction, and the proof is complete.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction to prove statements parametrized by n; show base case and then assume for n to prove for n+1. Often used for divisibility/recurrence properties and construction of infinite sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing the square / cube
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite polynomials by completing the square or cube to reveal structure (e.g., m6 + 2a0m4 + bm2 + c = (m3 + a0m)2 + (b − a0^2)m2 + c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completion to compare an expression to consecutive perfect powers, bound it between consecutive squares/cubes for large parameters, or obtain Diophantine constraints limiting solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity arguments and parity-changing substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parity of coefficients or variables to reduce cases; change variables (n → n+1) to switch parity and reduce odd/even cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate even/odd cases early; sometimes a variable shift flips parity and reduces the odd-case to the even-case (or vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of parameter to avoid perfect powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose parameters (e.g., n a prime not dividing b or n = m^2) so that an expression is not a perfect square/cube infinitely often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct families (by letting a parameter be prime, a perfect power, or large) to ensure only finitely many coincidences with perfect powers, hence obtain infinitely many admissible choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the pigeonhole principle for residues/divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Among n+1 numbers of certain form there are two with the same residue mod n, producing a repunit divisible by n (argument used for repunits and base-10 divisibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare residues of specially formed numbers (like repunits) to force the existence of divisible elements; typical in digit/divisibility problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization pattern of repunits
rubrics_metrics.description: If a repunit has m×n digits with m,n>1 then it factors as a product of smaller repunits/tens-powers, so a repunit can be prime only if its number of digits is prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit algebraic factorization of (10^{mn}-1)/(9) to detect compositeness and reason about primality of repunits; converses may fail (not every repunit with prime length is prime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Fermat's little theorem and multiplicative order
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the minimal n such that 10^n ≡ 1 (mod p) by noting n divides p−1 (or appropriate totient), then check divisors (example: repunit divisible by 19 => minimal n divides 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to checking divisors of the group order to find minimal exponents, using small exponent tests to eliminate possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit-sum and modulo 9 reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use that a number ≡ sum of its digits (mod 9) to constrain possible digit sums or residues of constructed large numbers (used to deduce small possibilities for digit-sum B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine bounds on number of digits with digit-sum congruence modulo 9 to pin down a small list of possible values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base expansion methods (binary, ternary, base p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with base representations (binary/ternary/other) to capture structural properties: count digits, describe functions on digits, construct Cantor-set mappings, or translate digit constraints into algebraic statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate problems about digits or digit-based functions into statements about digit sequences; use termination/recurrence on digits and induction on length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of transformations mapping solutions to other solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Find involutions or maps (e.g., (x,y)→(y−x,−x), (m,n)→(n−m,m), or (yz−x,y,z)) that transform solutions into other solutions and reduce size to reach base cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such maps to perform descent or to generate all solutions from a fundamental one by iterating inverse transformations; verify termination and uniqueness of base solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize sequences via linear recurrences (Fibonacci-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that sequences of solutions satisfy linear recurrences (e.g., an+1 = 3an − an−1, linking to Fibonacci numbers), enabling identification of all solutions as Fibonacci-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive recurrence from the transformation that generates new solutions and match initial terms to known sequences to obtain closed-form characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quadratic/cubic residue classes mod small moduli to eliminate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce equations modulo primes (e.g., mod 9, 11, 13, 17) and use known sets of quadratic/cubic/quartic residues to show impossibility of congruences (example: residue 7 mod 13 not expressible as cube+fourth power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moduli where the set of k-th power residues is small or structured (often p with (p−1) divisible by relevant exponents) to get contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group-order/divisibility considerations to limit residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick modulus where multiplicative group's order factors align with exponents (e.g., 13 with order 12=3×4), so cubes and fourth powers lie in small subgroups and residues are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This refines residue checks: compute subgroup orders and list possible residues to detect impossible target residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite descent via prime divisibility forcing all variables divisible
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a prime dividing some combination forces divisibility of all variables, contradicting coprimality (e.g., residues mod 7 force each variable to be divisible by 7, contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use residue analysis to infer that each variable must be divisible by a prime, then reduce to contradiction or infinite descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding with inequalities and digit-count/log estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inequalities and approximations (logs, digit counts) to bound magnitude, number of digits, or compare expressions (e.g., bound number of digits of 44444444 to limit digit-sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive upper/lower bounds on numbers of digits or size to reduce search or limit possible sums/digits; combine with congruences for a tight conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pell-type reductions via completing the square
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply and rearrange Diophantine equations to a Pell-type (Ax^2 − By^2 = C) and then analyze residues or solvability mod B to rule out solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard step: clear denominators/multiply by constant and complete the square to seek Pell-form; then use quadratic residue theory mod B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of explicit constructions to produce infinitely many examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct infinite families by embedding divisibility patterns (e.g., multiply a base factor by an appropriate perfect square to adjust number of digits while preserving divisibility; repunit families from 10^{(2k+1)11}+1 divisible by 121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine base congruences and multiplication by perfect powers to scale examples into desired numerical ranges, producing infinite families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting combinatorial digit patterns (palindromes, runs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count numbers with given digital patterns via combinatorics (e.g., number of binary palindromes of length k is 2^{(k−1)/2}, count of numbers with specified pairs of differing bits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model binary/decimal digit constraints as free choices in specified positions; use combinatorial formulas to count possibilities and subtract excluded ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invert-digit operations and characterize fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and analyze digit-manipulating functions (e.g., function f that reverses binary digits) to identify fixed points as palindromic numbers and count them under bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove operation properties by induction on digit-length and use the digit-level description to enumerate fixed points (palindromes) up to a bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor-set / Lebesgue construction for continuous surjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a continuous onto map from [0,1] to the square by coding coordinates in ternary expansion restricted to the Cantor set and linearly extend over removed intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define mapping on Cantor set via splitting ternary digits into two binary sequences for coordinates, then extend linearly across removed middle-thirds to get a continuous surjection with prescribed properties (e.g., no fixed point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive sequence construction avoiding arithmetic progressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct sequence {b_n} by writing n in base (p−1) and reading in base p; use properties that subtracting certain d avoids creating p-term arithmetic progressions and prove minimality/uniqueness by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove structure: digits p−1 in base-p correspond to membership/exclusion and employ digit-wise manipulations to ensure no p-term progression; use induction to show constructed sequence matches greedy minimal construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of digit-manipulation algorithms with squeeze arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functions algorithmically based on digit tail structure and use monotonicity and squeezing among neighboring digit-patterns to force unique assigned values (examples in base-3 mapping and decimal digit algorithms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove correctness by comparing with neighboring extremal patterns and employing monotonicity to force the only consistent value, completing induction on digit structure.
